standard.title: Layers of meaning through literary devices
standard.description: understand how layers of meaning can be created when evaluating by using literary devices such as simile and metaphor
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify evaluative language that expresses opinions and judgements, and understand how word choice signals attitude (AC9E7LA02). They have not yet examined how rhetorical devices such as irony, hyperbole, parody and understatement create layered meaning that separates surface statement from implied meaning.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how literary and rhetorical devices create layers of meaning when evaluating, including how devices like irony and hyperbole enable a speaker or writer to mean something different from or beyond what is literally stated.

nodes.label: Devices that separate surface and implied meaning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify rhetorical devices (irony, hyperbole, parody, understatement) and explain that they create a gap between what is literally said and what is meant.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one rhetorical device (e.g. irony or hyperbole) in a provided text and explain that the surface statement and the implied meaning are different.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain how irony, hyperbole, parody and understatement each create a gap between literal statement and implied meaning, drawing on examples from a range of texts including speeches, opinion pieces or humorous writing.
wider: Compare how two different devices (e.g. understatement vs hyperbole) achieve contrasting evaluative effects on the same subject in two different texts
Investigate how political cartoons or satirical writing use parody and irony simultaneously to layer multiple evaluative meanings
Examine how First Nations or non-Western rhetorical traditions use indirect or figurative expression to convey serious social or political commentary

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate irony with sarcasm, or miss understatement as a device. Encountering these devices across varied text types (humour, political commentary, literature) resolves device-specific misconceptions through broader exposure.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of rhetorical devices and the variety of texts that deploy them — from political satire to everyday humour to literary fiction — provides rich comparative ground that extends well beyond minimum identification.
success_criteria: Names a rhetorical device and identifies where it appears in a specific text.
Explains the difference between the literal statement and the implied or intended meaning created by the device.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate irony with sarcasm or cannot identify understatement arrive at Node 2 unable to explain how devices layer meaning — you cannot analyse the layering of a device you cannot reliably identify. Systematic device misidentification makes Node 2's integration task incoherent.

nodes.label: Devices creating layers in evaluative texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how literary and rhetorical devices work together in evaluative writing to create meaning that exceeds the literal content — including how dark or serious subjects can be treated through humour.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one device in an evaluative text (e.g. an opinion piece or review) contributes to a layered reading — where the device adds meaning beyond what a literal reading would yield.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how multiple devices operate together in evaluative texts to create layered meaning, including how authors use humour, irony or exaggeration to illuminate serious issues without stating them directly.
wider: Analyse how a piece of sustained satire (e.g. a satirical news article or speech) deploys multiple devices to simultaneously entertain and critique
Compare how simile and metaphor operate differently from irony and hyperbole in evaluative contexts — one layer of figurative meaning vs an inverted relationship to literal meaning
Write a short evaluative piece that uses at least two devices to create layered meaning, then annotate to explain the effect

response_modes.reason: Students need to hold two levels simultaneously — what a text says and what it implies — and see how multiple devices can layer these relationships. This integration of device knowledge into evaluative reading is the descriptor's core demand.

success_criteria: Explains how a specific device creates meaning beyond the literal content in an evaluative text.
Uses appropriate metalanguage (e.g. 'irony', 'hyperbole', 'understatement') accurately in written explanation.
